title: Trump's DHS Pick Came With Warnings About More FEMA Cuts
description_short: Trump's DHS Pick Came With Warnings About More FEMA Cuts
description_medium: The Guardian reported fears that Markwayne Mullin would bring further FEMA cuts and weaker readiness to a department already stretched thin. This matters because disaster response is one of the least glamorous ways cruelty shows up in government. You do not need a viral quote to hurt people; sometimes you just hollow out the agency they will need when everything floods, burns, or blows apart.
description_long: At his March 2026 confirmation hearing to lead the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin faced questions about FEMA after Kristi Noem proposed eliminating the agency and personally reviewing some of its larger expenditures. Mullin said FEMA should be “restructured, not eliminated,” criticized the spending reviews as micromanagement and said he would find a qualified head for the agency. He did not commit to ending the staff reductions already underway or say whether FEMA was overstaffed; he promised it would be adequately staffed to respond to disasters. The Guardian reported that FEMA had gone without a Senate-confirmed administrator during Trump’s second term to that point. A former FEMA chief of staff welcomed Mullin’s opposition to micromanagement but said readiness would depend on his actions after confirmation. The article also cited a Government Accountability Office warning that limited workforce capacity was compromising disaster preparedness and a FEMA manager’s account that the agency lost 10% of its workforce in the first half of 2025. The hearing recorded concerns and commitments, not a completed staffing plan or a documented disaster-response failure.

title: Trump's EPA Let Industry Science Weaken Formaldehyde Cancer Rules
description_short: Trump's EPA Let Industry Science Weaken Formaldehyde Cancer Rules
description_medium: Documents showed Trump's EPA relying on industry-backed science to weaken formaldehyde cancer rules, reversing stricter public-health limits. This is the kind of slow violence the administration excels at: nothing explodes on camera, but toxic exposure rules get sanded down until ordinary people carry more risk and corporations carry less inconvenience.
description_long: Documents obtained by the Environmental Defense Fund through a public-records request traced how the Trump administration changed the EPA’s formaldehyde risk assessment. In late 2024, the Biden-era EPA had concluded that any inhaled exposure to formaldehyde increased cancer and other health risks. In late 2025, the Trump EPA replaced that assessment with a higher threshold, setting the level at which it said cancer risk begins at 0.3 parts per million. The Guardian reported that the revised analysis relied in part on studies led by chemical-industry scientist Rory Conolly, funded by trade groups and previously judged outdated or unreliable by the EPA. The documents also described a 2023 meeting between EPA officials, formaldehyde producers, users and trade groups, with Conolly among the presenters. The EPA defended its assessment, saying the previous administration used flawed analyses and that the new review relied on “gold standard science.” Formaldehyde is used in products including furniture, cosmetics and craft supplies, and chemical makers produce billions of pounds annually. The report describes a regulatory change and competing accounts of its scientific basis; it does not measure resulting exposures or illnesses.

title: Trump's Crackdown Chased a Tufts Student All the Way Through Her Degree
description_short: Trump's Crackdown Chased a Tufts Student All the Way Through Her Degree
description_medium: Rümeysa Öztürk, the Tufts doctoral student detained by ICE after co-writing a pro-Palestinian campus op-ed, completed her PhD and returned to Turkey in April 2026. A settlement resolved her federal litigation, reinstated her student status and allowed her return without administration interference. The report says government records contained no evidence beyond the op-ed for revoking her visa and seeking deportation.
description_long: In March 2024, Rümeysa Öztürk and three Tufts classmates co-wrote an op-ed calling on the university to acknowledge what they described as a genocide of Palestinians. A year later, the Trump administration revoked Öztürk’s student visa, and masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested her in Massachusetts and transferred her to a Louisiana detention center. She was placed in deportation proceedings and fought the case in court. The Guardian reported that an immigration judge later terminated her case, finding no grounds for deportation, and that the administration appealed. In April 2026, after completing her doctorate, Öztürk returned to Turkey. She and the government had reached a settlement that resolved outstanding federal litigation; both sides asked for her immigration case to be dismissed. The agreement restored her student status and allowed her to leave without interference from the administration. The article also cited government records obtained in a separate lawsuit against Secretary of State Marco Rubio, which showed no evidence beyond the campus op-ed to support revoking her visa and pursuing deportation. Öztürk said she would continue her academic career in child study and human development. The sequence documents detention, litigation and settlement, as well as the eventual end of the deportation case.

title: Trump Told Astronauts He Saved NASA While Trying to Gut It
description_short: Trump Told Astronauts He Saved NASA While Trying to Gut It
description_medium: Astronauts had a call with the US president from space after setting record for the farthest-traveled humans from Earth. The lie mattered because it captured a recurring Trump move: bask in the prestige of institutions and scientific achievements he is simultaneously trying to starve, shrink, or break.
description_long: During a call with the Artemis II crew near the Moon, Donald Trump said he had chosen to revive NASA rather than close it during his first term. The Guardian set that claim against the administration’s funding proposals. Trump directed more resources to NASA’s human-spaceflight program, including Artemis, while the White House proposed a 24% cut to the agency’s overall budget, to $18.8 billion. Congress later passed a $24.4 billion budget that was almost fully funded. Two days after Artemis II launched, Trump released a 2027 budget request seeking another 23% reduction, including deep cuts to NASA science programs. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman backed the efficiency agenda and urged agency employees to focus on the mission. The call itself included praise for the astronauts’ record-setting journey and plans for U.S. space exploration. The documented contrast is between Trump’s claim that he rescued NASA and budget proposals that would reduce its overall resources even as his administration supported human-spaceflight projects. The article describes a proposal for fiscal year 2027, not an enacted cut.

title: Trump Turned Another Arizona Rally Into a Fog of War Boasts and Familiar Nonsense
description_short: Trump Turned Another Arizona Rally Into a Fog of War Boasts and Familiar Nonsense
description_medium: With an appearance at a Turning Point USA event at a megachurch Arizona, President Trump is hitting the campaign trail in front of a friendly crowd at a time his approval ratings are at record lows. That belongs in the catalog because Trump's rally style is not just boastful. It is a recurring attempt to blur war, spectacle, grievance, and fantasy into one flattering fog around himself.
